40	
41	## Core Problem
42	
43	LLM agents can be jailbroken through sequences of individually-benign tool calls that compose into harmful operations — STAC (arXiv 2509.25624) achieves >90% ASR on GPT-4.1 via this — yet existing defenses either operate at the wrong granularity (step-level guardrails like ToolSafe miss cross-step compositional intent; prompt-level detectors like RLM-JB analyze input text, not execution traces), rely on manually-authored rules that cannot generalize to novel compositions (AgentArmor's type system at ICLR 2026, Agent-Sentry's structural classifier with allowlists, ARGUS's provenance-based verification, SMT solvers), target the wrong graph type (G-Guard/GuardNet reason over text entity graphs; BlindGuard/XG-Guard/G-Safeguard model MAS inter-agent communication graphs, not intra-agent tool-call dependencies), or operate at the wrong stage (MindGuard's DDGs detect tool-poisoning pre-execution via attention flows but cannot detect compositional harm that emerges only from post-execution data-flow composition of benign calls). No learned defense reasons over tool-call dependency graphs to detect distributed malicious intent emerging from benign compositions.
44	
45	## Opportunity / Why Now
46	
47	STAC (arXiv 2509.25624, Sep 2025; benchmark open-sourced at amazon-science/MultiTurnAgentAttack) provides ready-made evaluation for compositional tool-chain attacks (483 cases, 1352 interactions, 10 failure modes) with an automated generation pipeline that can be repurposed to create additional synthetic attack traces for both pre-training and fine-tuning augmentation. Its best prompt-based defense reduces ASR by only 28.8%. The trace-based defense space has matured rapidly — AgentArmor (ICLR 2026) constructs PDGs with rule-based type systems, Agent-Sentry (Mar 2026) layers structural classifiers with provenance-aware allowlists, ARGUS (May 2026) uses provenance graphs for decision auditing, MindGuard (Jan 2026) uses attention-flow DDGs for pre-execution tool-poisoning detection — but all are rule-based or attention-based and cannot generalize to unseen compositional patterns that emerge post-execution. Meanwhile, graph-based anomaly detection for MAS has advanced (G-Safeguard at ACL 2025, BlindGuard at ACL 2026 with corruption-guided contrastive learning), but none target single-agent tool-call composition. TraceSafe (Apr 2026) explicitly identifies 'structural bottleneck' as the key challenge for trajectory guardrails, motivating graph-structural approaches. Supervised contrastive learning (Khosla et al., NeurIPS 2020) demonstrates superior data efficiency over cross-entropy in reduced-data regimes, and label contrastive coding for graph classification (LCGNN, arXiv 2101.05486) verifies this advantage extends to graph-level tasks — making supervised contrastive pre-training viable even with moderate corpus sizes. EMNLP 2026 (ARR submission deadline: May 25, 2026) is an appropriate venue under the 'LLM Agents' area.
48	
49	## Landscape (SOTA & Limitations)
50	
51	STAC (arXiv 2509.25624, Sep 2025; withdrawn from ICLR 2026 but benchmark remains open-source) demonstrates that chaining benign tool calls achieves >90% ASR even on GPT-4.1; its best prompt-based defense reduces ASR by only 28.8%. ToolSafe (arXiv 2601.10156, Jan 2026) trains an RL-based step-level guardrail with interpretable feedback (TS-Guard) but reasons per-step rather than over full graph structure. RLM-JB (arXiv 2602.16520, Feb 2026) uses recursive language models for jailbreak detection but operates on INPUT TEXT, not tool-call execution traces. AgentArmor (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2508.01249) constructs program dependency graphs (PDGs) and applies a type-system-based inspector, reducing ASR to 3% on AgentDojo — but targets indirect prompt injection with a rule-based type system that cannot generalize to novel compositions. Agent-Sentry (arXiv 2603.22868, Mar 2026) uses structural classifier + allowlist + LLM judge — fundamentally rule-based, targeting prompt injection. ARGUS (arXiv 2605.03378, May 2026) constructs influence provenance graphs with rule-based verification for context-aware prompt injection. MindGuard (arXiv 2508.20412, Jan 2026) constructs Decision Dependence Graphs (DDGs) from LLM attention flows for tool-poisoning defense — achieving 94-99% detection precision — but operates pre-execution on attention patterns, uses empirical thresholds rather than learned representations, and targets tool metadata poisoning where the threat is in the tool description, not compositional harm emerging from execution-level data-flow between benign calls. G-Guard (arXiv 2507.07146) uses GCN on text entity graphs. GuardNet (arXiv 2509.23037) achieves 99.8% F1 via hierarchical GNN over token graphs. In the MAS defense space, G-Safeguard (ACL 2025) applies supervised GNN on multi-agent communication topology; BlindGuard (ACL 2026, arXiv 2508.08127) uses unsupervised corruption-guided contrastive learning on hierarchical agent graphs — its corruption-guided detection paradigm directly inspires our approach but operates on inter-agent communication, not tool-call dependencies. XG-Guard (arXiv 2512.18733) uses bi-level GNN for explainable MAS anomaly detection. IPIGuard (EMNLP 2025) constructs tool dependency graphs but targets indirect prompt injection via pre-planned execution. TraceSafe (arXiv 2604.07223, Apr 2026) benchmarks mid-trajectory guardrails and finds structural data competence matters more than semantic safety alignment. The key gap: all existing trace/provenance-based defenses (AgentArmor, Agent-Sentry, ARGUS, MindGuard) are RULE-BASED or THRESHOLD-BASED and cannot generalize to unseen compositional patterns; no LEARNED model reasons over tool-call data-flow dependency graphs to detect compositional jailbreaks where each individual tool invocation is benign.
52	
53	## Proposed Approach
54	
55	We propose CompGraph, a supervised contrastive graph learning framework that detects compositional jailbreaks in tool-augmented LLM agents by reasoning over tool-call dependency graphs. The approach has four components:
56	
57	(1) GRAPH CONSTRUCTION: From agent execution traces (STAC format), we construct directed acyclic graphs where nodes represent individual tool invocations and edges capture three types of dependencies: data-flow (output-to-input value propagation), temporal ordering, and argument overlap (shared entities/values across calls). Each node is encoded via frozen Qwen3-Embedding-8B (MTEB #1 multilingual embedding model, 4096-dim) applied to a concatenation of tool name, serialized arguments, and return value summary. We use a general-purpose embedding model rather than a safety classifier — since STAC attacks use individually benign tool calls, a safety-tuned encoder would produce near-identical 'safe' embeddings for all nodes, destroying discriminative signal.
58	
59	(2) CORRUPTION-GUIDED CONTRASTIVE PRE-TRAINING: We construct a pre-training corpus of ~5000 benign tool-call graphs (randomly composed from STAC's tool inventory) plus ~2000 synthetic attack graphs (generated via STAC's automated generation pipeline). A 3-layer MPNN encoder with graph-level mean-pooling readout is trained via supervised contrastive loss (SupCon; Khosla et al., NeurIPS 2020): positive pairs are augmented views of same-class graphs (node feature masking, edge dropping, subgraph sampling); negative pairs are cross-class graphs. Crucially, we apply three formally-defined corruption operators to benign graphs as hard negatives:
60	
61	   (a) DATA-FLOW REROUTING: For a benign edge (tool_i → tool_j), redirect the data-flow to a sensitive tool_k where tool_k ∈ {send_email, http_post, write_external_file, api_call_external}. This simulates STAC's 'data exfiltration' and 'unauthorized communication' failure modes by creating chains where benign data-gathering feeds into exfiltration endpoints.
62	
63	   (b) CHAIN EXTENSION: Append a terminal exfiltration node to an existing benign subgraph's leaf node, connecting via a data-flow edge that propagates the leaf's output. The appended node is sampled from a sensitive-tool vocabulary. This simulates STAC's 'information leakage' and 'privacy violation' failure modes.
64	
65	   (c) ARGUMENT INJECTION: Identify sensitive argument values (API keys, file paths containing 'credentials'/'password'/'secret', PII fields) in one subgraph and copy them into an unrelated tool call's arguments in a different subgraph, creating a cross-subgraph data-flow edge. This simulates STAC's 'credential misuse' and 'unauthorized access' failure modes.
66	
67	   Each corruption operator maps to 2-3 of STAC's 10 failure modes, and we validate that corrupted graphs are structurally similar to real attack graphs by measuring graph edit distance between corruptions and held-out STAC attacks (requiring mean GED within 1σ of intra-attack-class GED). This ensures corruptions produce realistic hard negatives rather than unrealistic graph structures.
68	
69	   We justify this supervised contrastive approach on data-efficiency grounds: unlike self-supervised GCL — which requires >4,000 graphs to outperform untrained baselines by a modest ~2% ROC-AUC (arXiv 2509.01541) — supervised contrastive learning with explicit class labels provides direct optimization signal, demonstrating superior data efficiency over cross-entropy in reduced-data regimes (Khosla et al., NeurIPS 2020). LCGNN (arXiv 2101.05486) confirms this advantage extends to graph-level classification, achieving faster convergence and lower loss with the same training data. Our pre-training corpus of ~7000 graphs with explicit class labels operates in a fundamentally different efficiency regime than self-supervised GCL.
70	
71	(3) FEW-SHOT-AWARE FINE-TUNING: With only 483 labeled STAC samples (averaging ~48 per failure mode, likely imbalanced), standard supervised fine-tuning risks overfitting. We adopt a three-pronged strategy:
72	
73	   (a) LINEAR PROBE (primary): Freeze the pre-trained MPNN encoder entirely and train only a lightweight classification head (2-layer MLP) on STAC's labeled data. This reduces trainable parameters by >95% and prevents catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained representations.
74	
75	   (b) PROTOTYPE-BASED CLASSIFICATION (alternative): Compute mean graph embedding per class (benign vs. each failure mode) from support examples, classify test graphs via nearest-prototype in embedding space. This requires zero gradient updates at inference and naturally handles class imbalance.
76	
77	   (c) AUGMENTED FINE-TUNING (scaling): Use STAC's automated pipeline to generate ~500 additional labeled attack traces (validated through in-environment execution), expanding the fine-tuning set to ~1000 labeled samples. We report results both with and without augmentation to isolate the contribution of additional data.
78	
79	   We compare all three strategies and report which achieves best ASR reduction vs. FPR tradeoff.
80	
81	(4) SUPERVISED CLASSIFICATION: The fine-tuned system outputs binary safe/unsafe prediction plus auxiliary 10-way failure-mode classification (when using the MLP head). We use stratified splitting by failure mode for evaluation.
82	
83	Evaluation: (a) In-distribution: held-out STAC splits (stratified by failure mode), reporting ASR reduction and detection F1. (b) Cross-failure-mode generalization: hold out 2-3 of STAC's 10 failure modes during training and evaluate on held-out modes — testing whether learned graph representations capture transferable compositional structure. (c) False positive rate on benign traces from STAC's baseline runs. (d) Baselines: (i) STAC's reasoning-driven defense prompt (best existing, 28.8% ASR reduction), (ii) ToolSafe's step-level TS-Guard, (iii) Weisfeiler-Leman subtree kernel + SVM on tool-call graphs, (iv) hand-crafted graph features (depth, branching factor, data-flow chain length, argument overlap density, tool fanout, sensitive-tool reachability, cross-subgraph data-flow count) + random forest, (v) MPNN from scratch (no pre-training) with linear probe, (vi) self-supervised GraphCL pre-training + linear probe ablation (to directly compare supervised vs. self-supervised contrastive), (vii) SupCon without corruption augmentations ablation (to isolate corruption contribution). We target competitive ASR reduction with <5% FPR on benign traces.
84	
85	The key contribution is methodological: we formalize tool-call dependency graph construction from execution traces, define semantically-grounded corruption operators that generate realistic hard negatives mapped to known failure modes, and demonstrate that supervised contrastive graph learning with few-shot-aware fine-tuning captures compositional attack patterns invisible to step-level, prompt-level, rule-based, or attention-based defenses.
86	
87	## Resource Estimate
88

## Core Problem

LLM agents can be jailbroken through sequences of individually-benign tool calls that compose into harmful operations — STAC (arXiv 2509.25624) achieves >90% ASR on GPT-4.1 via this — yet existing defenses either operate at the wrong granularity (step-level guardrails like ToolSafe miss cross-step compositional intent; prompt-level detectors like RLM-JB analyze input text, not execution traces), rely on manually-authored rules that cannot generalize to novel compositions (AgentArmor's type system at ICLR 2026, Agent-Sentry's structural classifier with allowlists, ARGUS's provenance-based verification, SMT solvers), target the wrong graph type (G-Guard/GuardNet reason over text entity graphs; BlindGuard/XG-Guard/G-Safeguard model MAS inter-agent communication graphs, not intra-agent tool-call dependencies), or operate at the wrong stage (MindGuard's DDGs detect tool-poisoning pre-execution via attention flows but cannot detect compositional harm that emerges only from post-execution data-flow composition of benign calls). No learned defense reasons over tool-call dependency graphs to detect distributed malicious intent emerging from benign compositions.

## Opportunity / Why Now

STAC (arXiv 2509.25624, Sep 2025; benchmark open-sourced at amazon-science/MultiTurnAgentAttack) provides ready-made evaluation for compositional tool-chain attacks (483 cases, 1352 interactions, 10 failure modes) with an automated generation pipeline that can be repurposed to create additional synthetic attack traces for both pre-training and fine-tuning augmentation. Its best prompt-based defense reduces ASR by only 28.8%. The trace-based defense space has matured rapidly — AgentArmor (ICLR 2026) constructs PDGs with rule-based type systems, Agent-Sentry (Mar 2026) layers structural classifiers with provenance-aware allowlists, ARGUS (May 2026) uses provenance graphs for decision auditing, MindGuard (Jan 2026) uses attention-flow DDGs for pre-execution tool-poisoning detection — but all are rule-based or attention-based and cannot generalize to unseen compositional patterns that emerge post-execution. Meanwhile, graph-based anomaly detection for MAS has advanced (G-Safeguard at ACL 2025, BlindGuard at ACL 2026 with corruption-guided contrastive learning), but none target single-agent tool-call composition. TraceSafe (Apr 2026) explicitly identifies 'structural bottleneck' as the key challenge for trajectory guardrails, motivating graph-structural approaches. Supervised contrastive learning (Khosla et al., NeurIPS 2020) demonstrates superior data efficiency over cross-entropy in reduced-data regimes, and label contrastive coding for graph classification (LCGNN, arXiv 2101.05486) verifies this advantage extends to graph-level tasks — making supervised contrastive pre-training viable even with moderate corpus sizes. EMNLP 2026 (ARR submission deadline: May 25, 2026) is an appropriate venue under the 'LLM Agents' area.

## Landscape (SOTA & Limitations)

STAC (arXiv 2509.25624, Sep 2025; withdrawn from ICLR 2026 but benchmark remains open-source) demonstrates that chaining benign tool calls achieves >90% ASR even on GPT-4.1; its best prompt-based defense reduces ASR by only 28.8%. ToolSafe (arXiv 2601.10156, Jan 2026) trains an RL-based step-level guardrail with interpretable feedback (TS-Guard) but reasons per-step rather than over full graph structure. RLM-JB (arXiv 2602.16520, Feb 2026) uses recursive language models for jailbreak detection but operates on INPUT TEXT, not tool-call execution traces. AgentArmor (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2508.01249) constructs program dependency graphs (PDGs) and applies a type-system-based inspector, reducing ASR to 3% on AgentDojo — but targets indirect prompt injection with a rule-based type system that cannot generalize to novel compositions. Agent-Sentry (arXiv 2603.22868, Mar 2026) uses structural classifier + allowlist + LLM judge — fundamentally rule-based, targeting prompt injection. ARGUS (arXiv 2605.03378, May 2026) constructs influence provenance graphs with rule-based verification for context-aware prompt injection. MindGuard (arXiv 2508.20412, Jan 2026) constructs Decision Dependence Graphs (DDGs) from LLM attention flows for tool-poisoning defense — achieving 94-99% detection precision — but operates pre-execution on attention patterns, uses empirical thresholds rather than learned representations, and targets tool metadata poisoning where the threat is in the tool description, not compositional harm emerging from execution-level data-flow between benign calls. G-Guard (arXiv 2507.07146) uses GCN on text entity graphs. GuardNet (arXiv 2509.23037) achieves 99.8% F1 via hierarchical GNN over token graphs. In the MAS defense space, G-Safeguard (ACL 2025) applies supervised GNN on multi-agent communication topology; BlindGuard (ACL 2026, arXiv 2508.08127) uses unsupervised corruption-guided contrastive learning on hierarchical agent graphs — its corruption-guided detection paradigm directly inspires our approach but operates on inter-agent communication, not tool-call dependencies. XG-Guard (arXiv 2512.18733) uses bi-level GNN for explainable MAS anomaly detection. IPIGuard (EMNLP 2025) constructs tool dependency graphs but targets indirect prompt injection via pre-planned execution. TraceSafe (arXiv 2604.07223, Apr 2026) benchmarks mid-trajectory guardrails and finds structural data competence matters more than semantic safety alignment. The key gap: all existing trace/provenance-based defenses (AgentArmor, Agent-Sentry, ARGUS, MindGuard) are RULE-BASED or THRESHOLD-BASED and cannot generalize to unseen compositional patterns; no LEARNED model reasons over tool-call data-flow dependency graphs to detect compositional jailbreaks where each individual tool invocation is benign.

## Proposed Approach

We propose CompGraph, a supervised contrastive graph learning framework that detects compositional jailbreaks in tool-augmented LLM agents by reasoning over tool-call dependency graphs. The approach has four components:

(1) GRAPH CONSTRUCTION: From agent execution traces (STAC format), we construct directed acyclic graphs where nodes represent individual tool invocations and edges capture three types of dependencies: data-flow (output-to-input value propagation), temporal ordering, and argument overlap (shared entities/values across calls). Each node is encoded via frozen Qwen3-Embedding-8B (MTEB #1 multilingual embedding model, 4096-dim) applied to a concatenation of tool name, serialized arguments, and return value summary. We use a general-purpose embedding model rather than a safety classifier — since STAC attacks use individually benign tool calls, a safety-tuned encoder would produce near-identical 'safe' embeddings for all nodes, destroying discriminative signal.

(2) CORRUPTION-GUIDED CONTRASTIVE PRE-TRAINING: We construct a pre-training corpus of ~5000 benign tool-call graphs (randomly composed from STAC's tool inventory) plus ~2000 synthetic attack graphs (generated via STAC's automated generation pipeline). A 3-layer MPNN encoder with graph-level mean-pooling readout is trained via supervised contrastive loss (SupCon; Khosla et al., NeurIPS 2020): positive pairs are augmented views of same-class graphs (node feature masking, edge dropping, subgraph sampling); negative pairs are cross-class graphs. Crucially, we apply three formally-defined corruption operators to benign graphs as hard negatives:

   (a) DATA-FLOW REROUTING: For a benign edge (tool_i → tool_j), redirect the data-flow to a sensitive tool_k where tool_k ∈ {send_email, http_post, write_external_file, api_call_external}. This simulates STAC's 'data exfiltration' and 'unauthorized communication' failure modes by creating chains where benign data-gathering feeds into exfiltration endpoints.

   (b) CHAIN EXTENSION: Append a terminal exfiltration node to an existing benign subgraph's leaf node, connecting via a data-flow edge that propagates the leaf's output. The appended node is sampled from a sensitive-tool vocabulary. This simulates STAC's 'information leakage' and 'privacy violation' failure modes.

   (c) ARGUMENT INJECTION: Identify sensitive argument values (API keys, file paths containing 'credentials'/'password'/'secret', PII fields) in one subgraph and copy them into an unrelated tool call's arguments in a different subgraph, creating a cross-subgraph data-flow edge. This simulates STAC's 'credential misuse' and 'unauthorized access' failure modes.

   Each corruption operator maps to 2-3 of STAC's 10 failure modes, and we validate that corrupted graphs are structurally similar to real attack graphs by measuring graph edit distance between corruptions and held-out STAC attacks (requiring mean GED within 1σ of intra-attack-class GED). This ensures corruptions produce realistic hard negatives rather than unrealistic graph structures.

   We justify this supervised contrastive approach on data-efficiency grounds: unlike self-supervised GCL — which requires >4,000 graphs to outperform untrained baselines by a modest ~2% ROC-AUC (arXiv 2509.01541) — supervised contrastive learning with explicit class labels provides direct optimization signal, demonstrating superior data efficiency over cross-entropy in reduced-data regimes (Khosla et al., NeurIPS 2020). LCGNN (arXiv 2101.05486) confirms this advantage extends to graph-level classification, achieving faster convergence and lower loss with the same training data. Our pre-training corpus of ~7000 graphs with explicit class labels operates in a fundamentally different efficiency regime than self-supervised GCL.

(3) FEW-SHOT-AWARE FINE-TUNING: With only 483 labeled STAC samples (averaging ~48 per failure mode, likely imbalanced), standard supervised fine-tuning risks overfitting. We adopt a three-pronged strategy:

   (a) LINEAR PROBE (primary): Freeze the pre-trained MPNN encoder entirely and train only a lightweight classification head (2-layer MLP) on STAC's labeled data. This reduces trainable parameters by >95% and prevents catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained representations.

   (b) PROTOTYPE-BASED CLASSIFICATION (alternative): Compute mean graph embedding per class (benign vs. each failure mode) from support examples, classify test graphs via nearest-prototype in embedding space. This requires zero gradient updates at inference and naturally handles class imbalance.

   (c) AUGMENTED FINE-TUNING (scaling): Use STAC's automated pipeline to generate ~500 additional labeled attack traces (validated through in-environment execution), expanding the fine-tuning set to ~1000 labeled samples. We report results both with and without augmentation to isolate the contribution of additional data.

   We compare all three strategies and report which achieves best ASR reduction vs. FPR tradeoff.

(4) SUPERVISED CLASSIFICATION: The fine-tuned system outputs binary safe/unsafe prediction plus auxiliary 10-way failure-mode classification (when using the MLP head). We use stratified splitting by failure mode for evaluation.

Evaluation: (a) In-distribution: held-out STAC splits (stratified by failure mode), reporting ASR reduction and detection F1. (b) Cross-failure-mode generalization: hold out 2-3 of STAC's 10 failure modes during training and evaluate on held-out modes — testing whether learned graph representations capture transferable compositional structure. (c) False positive rate on benign traces from STAC's baseline runs. (d) Baselines: (i) STAC's reasoning-driven defense prompt (best existing, 28.8% ASR reduction), (ii) ToolSafe's step-level TS-Guard, (iii) Weisfeiler-Leman subtree kernel + SVM on tool-call graphs, (iv) hand-crafted graph features (depth, branching factor, data-flow chain length, argument overlap density, tool fanout, sensitive-tool reachability, cross-subgraph data-flow count) + random forest, (v) MPNN from scratch (no pre-training) with linear probe, (vi) self-supervised GraphCL pre-training + linear probe ablation (to directly compare supervised vs. self-supervised contrastive), (vii) SupCon without corruption augmentations ablation (to isolate corruption contribution). We target competitive ASR reduction with <5% FPR on benign traces.

The key contribution is methodological: we formalize tool-call dependency graph construction from execution traces, define semantically-grounded corruption operators that generate realistic hard negatives mapped to known failure modes, and demonstrate that supervised contrastive graph learning with few-shot-aware fine-tuning captures compositional attack patterns invisible to step-level, prompt-level, rule-based, or attention-based defenses.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch_geometric.nn import GINConv, global_mean_pool


class GINEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim: int, hidden_dim: int = 64, feat_dim: int = 128, num_layers: int = 3, dropout: float = 0.5):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_layers = num_layers
        self.dropout = dropout

        self.convs = nn.ModuleList()
        self.bns = nn.ModuleList()

        for i in range(num_layers):
            in_dim = input_dim if i == 0 else hidden_dim
            mlp = nn.Sequential(
                nn.Linear(in_dim, hidden_dim),
                nn.ReLU(),
                nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim),
            )
            self.convs.append(GINConv(mlp))
            self.bns.append(nn.BatchNorm1d(hidden_dim))

        self.projection = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, feat_dim),
        )

    def forward(self, data) -> torch.Tensor:
        x, edge_index, batch = data.x, data.edge_index, data.batch

        for i in range(self.num_layers):
            x = self.convs[i](x, edge_index)
            x = self.bns[i](x)
            x = F.relu(x)
            x = F.dropout(x, p=self.dropout, training=self.training)

        x = global_mean_pool(x, batch)
        x = self.projection(x)
        x = F.normalize(x, dim=-1)
        return x

import argparse
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, f1_score, precision_score, recall_score
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import CosineAnnealingLR
from torch_geometric.loader import DataLoader

from src.models.gin_encoder import GINEncoder
from src.models.supcon_loss import SupConLoss
from src.augmentations import dual_augment


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="MVP training: SupCon + Linear Probe for graph jailbreak detection")
    parser.add_argument("--data_dir", type=str, default="./data")
    parser.add_argument("--epochs", type=int, default=100)
    parser.add_argument("--lr", type=float, default=0.001)
    parser.add_argument("--hidden_dim", type=int, default=64)
    parser.add_argument("--feat_dim", type=int, default=128)
    parser.add_argument("--batch_size", type=int, default=32)
    parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    parser.add_argument("--holdout_mode", type=str, default=None, help="Failure mode to hold out for testing")
    parser.add_argument("--n_folds", type=int, default=5)
    parser.add_argument("--patience", type=int, default=20)
    parser.add_argument("--weight_decay", type=float, default=1e-4)
    parser.add_argument("--output_dir", type=str, default="./results")
    parser.add_argument("--aug1", type=str, default="dropout_edge")
    parser.add_argument("--aug2", type=str, default="drop_feature")
    return parser.parse_args()


def set_seed(seed):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)


def load_dataset(data_dir, holdout_mode=None):
    data_path = Path(data_dir)
    graphs = torch.load(data_path / "graphs.pt", weights_only=False)

    if holdout_mode is not None:
        train_graphs = [g for g in graphs if getattr(g, 'failure_mode', None) != holdout_mode]
        test_graphs = [g for g in graphs if getattr(g, 'failure_mode', None) == holdout_mode]
        return train_graphs, test_graphs

    return graphs, None


def train_supcon_epoch(encoder, loader, optimizer, loss_fn, aug1, aug2, device):
    encoder.train()
    total_loss = 0.0
    for batch in loader:
        batch = batch.to(device)
        view1, view2 = dual_augment(batch, aug1, aug2)
        view1 = view1.to(device)
        view2 = view2.to(device)

        z1 = encoder(view1)
        z2 = encoder(view2)

        features = torch.stack([z1, z2], dim=1)  # [bsz, 2, feat_dim]
        loss = loss_fn(features, batch.y)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        total_loss += loss.item() * z1.size(0)

    return total_loss / len(loader.dataset)


def train_linear_probe(encoder, train_loader, val_loader, feat_dim, device, epochs=50, lr=0.01):
    encoder.eval()
    classifier = nn.Linear(feat_dim, 2).to(device)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(classifier.parameters(), lr=lr)
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

    best_auroc = 0.0
    best_state = None

    for epoch in range(epochs):
        classifier.train()
        for batch in train_loader:
            batch = batch.to(device)
            with torch.no_grad():
                feats = encoder(batch)
            logits = classifier(feats)
            loss = criterion(logits, batch.y)
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()

        auroc = evaluate(encoder, classifier, val_loader, device)["auroc"]
        if auroc > best_auroc:
            best_auroc = auroc
            best_state = classifier.state_dict().copy()

    classifier.load_state_dict(best_state)
    return classifier


def evaluate(encoder, classifier, loader, device):
    encoder.eval()
    classifier.eval()
    all_probs = []
    all_labels = []

    with torch.no_grad():
        for batch in loader:
            batch = batch.to(device)
            feats = encoder(batch)
            logits = classifier(feats)
            probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=1)[:, 1]
            all_probs.append(probs.cpu())
            all_labels.append(batch.y.cpu())

    all_probs = torch.cat(all_probs).numpy()
    all_labels = torch.cat(all_labels).numpy()
    preds = (all_probs >= 0.5).astype(int)

    return {
        "auroc": roc_auc_score(all_labels, all_probs),
        "f1": f1_score(all_labels, preds),
        "precision": precision_score(all_labels, preds, zero_division=0),
        "recall": recall_score(all_labels, preds, zero_division=0),
    }


def run_fold(train_graphs, val_graphs, args, device, fold_idx):
    train_loader = DataLoader(train_graphs, batch_size=args.batch_size, shuffle=True)
    val_loader = DataLoader(val_graphs, batch_size=args.batch_size, shuffle=False)

    input_dim = train_graphs[0].x.size(1)
    encoder = GINEncoder(
        input_dim=input_dim,
        hidden_dim=args.hidden_dim,
        feat_dim=args.feat_dim,
    ).to(device)

    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(encoder.parameters(), lr=args.lr, weight_decay=args.weight_decay)
    scheduler = CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, T_max=args.epochs)
    loss_fn = SupConLoss(temperature=0.07)

    best_val_auroc = 0.0
    patience_counter = 0
    best_encoder_state = None

    # Phase 1: SupCon pre-training
    for epoch in range(args.epochs):
        train_loss = train_supcon_epoch(encoder, train_loader, optimizer, loss_fn, args.aug1, args.aug2, device)
        scheduler.step()

        # Quick linear eval for early stopping
        tmp_classifier = nn.Linear(args.feat_dim, 2).to(device)
        tmp_opt = torch.optim.Adam(tmp_classifier.parameters(), lr=0.01)
        criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
        encoder.eval()
        for _ in range(10):
            tmp_classifier.train()
            for batch in train_loader:
                batch = batch.to(device)
                with torch.no_grad():
                    feats = encoder(batch)
                logits = tmp_classifier(feats)
                loss = criterion(logits, batch.y)
                tmp_opt.zero_grad()
                loss.backward()
                tmp_opt.step()

        metrics = evaluate(encoder, tmp_classifier, val_loader, device)
        val_auroc = metrics["auroc"]

        if val_auroc > best_val_auroc:
            best_val_auroc = val_auroc
            best_encoder_state = {k: v.clone() for k, v in encoder.state_dict().items()}
            patience_counter = 0
        else:
            patience_counter += 1

        if patience_counter >= args.patience:
            break

    encoder.load_state_dict(best_encoder_state)

    # Phase 2: Linear probe
    classifier = train_linear_probe(encoder, train_loader, val_loader, args.feat_dim, device)

    val_metrics = evaluate(encoder, classifier, val_loader, device)

    # Save checkpoint
    os.makedirs(args.output_dir, exist_ok=True)
    torch.save(encoder.state_dict(), os.path.join(args.output_dir, f"encoder_fold{fold_idx}.pt"))

    return val_metrics


def main():
    args = parse_args()
    set_seed(args.seed)
    device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

    graphs, test_graphs = load_dataset(args.data_dir, args.holdout_mode)

    if test_graphs is not None:
        # Cross-failure-mode holdout
        labels = np.array([g.y.item() for g in graphs])
        skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=args.n_folds, shuffle=True, random_state=args.seed)
        fold_results = []

        for fold_idx, (train_idx, val_idx) in enumerate(skf.split(np.zeros(len(graphs)), labels)):
            train_graphs_fold = [graphs[i] for i in train_idx]
            val_graphs_fold = [graphs[i] for i in val_idx]
            metrics = run_fold(train_graphs_fold, val_graphs_fold, args, device, fold_idx)
            fold_results.append(metrics)
            print(f"Fold {fold_idx}: AUROC={metrics['auroc']:.4f} F1={metrics['f1']:.4f}")

        # Evaluate on holdout test set
        input_dim = graphs[0].x.size(1)
        encoder = GINEncoder(input_dim=input_dim, hidden_dim=args.hidden_dim, feat_dim=args.feat_dim).to(device)
        encoder.load_state_dict(torch.load(os.path.join(args.output_dir, "encoder_fold0.pt"), weights_only=False))

        test_loader = DataLoader(test_graphs, batch_size=args.batch_size, shuffle=False)
        train_loader = DataLoader(graphs, batch_size=args.batch_size, shuffle=True)
        classifier = train_linear_probe(encoder, train_loader, test_loader, args.feat_dim, device)
        test_metrics = evaluate(encoder, classifier, test_loader, device)
        print(f"Holdout test ({args.holdout_mode}): AUROC={test_metrics['auroc']:.4f} F1={test_metrics['f1']:.4f}")

    else:
        # Standard 5-fold CV
        labels = np.array([g.y.item() for g in graphs])
        skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=args.n_folds, shuffle=True, random_state=args.seed)
        fold_results = []

        for fold_idx, (train_idx, val_idx) in enumerate(skf.split(np.zeros(len(graphs)), labels)):
            train_graphs_fold = [graphs[i] for i in train_idx]
            val_graphs_fold = [graphs[i] for i in val_idx]
            metrics = run_fold(train_graphs_fold, val_graphs_fold, args, device, fold_idx)
            fold_results.append(metrics)
            print(f"Fold {fold_idx}: AUROC={metrics['auroc']:.4f} F1={metrics['f1']:.4f}")

        test_metrics = None

    # Aggregate results
    avg_metrics = {}
    for key in fold_results[0]:
        values = [r[key] for r in fold_results]
        avg_metrics[key] = {"mean": float(np.mean(values)), "std": float(np.std(values))}

    results = {
        "args": vars(args),
        "fold_results": fold_results,
        "avg_metrics": avg_metrics,
    }
    if test_metrics is not None:
        results["holdout_test"] = test_metrics

    os.makedirs(args.output_dir, exist_ok=True)
    with open(os.path.join(args.output_dir, "results.json"), "w") as f:
        json.dump(results, f, indent=2)

    print(f"\nAverage: AUROC={avg_metrics['auroc']['mean']:.4f}±{avg_metrics['auroc']['std']:.4f} "
          f"F1={avg_metrics['f1']['mean']:.4f}±{avg_metrics['f1']['std']:.4f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import torch
from torch_geometric.data import Data


def dropout_edge(data: Data, p: float = 0.2) -> Data:
    edge_index = data.edge_index
    num_edges = edge_index.size(1)
    mask = torch.rand(num_edges) >= p
    new_edge_index = edge_index[:, mask]

    new_data = Data(x=data.x.clone(), edge_index=new_edge_index, batch=data.batch)
    if hasattr(data, 'y'):
        new_data.y = data.y
    return new_data


def drop_feature(data: Data, p: float = 0.2) -> Data:
    x = data.x.clone()
    feat_dim = x.size(1)
    mask = torch.rand(feat_dim) >= p
    x[:, ~mask] = 0.0

    new_data = Data(x=x, edge_index=data.edge_index.clone(), batch=data.batch)
    if hasattr(data, 'y'):
        new_data.y = data.y
    return new_data


def subgraph(data: Data, ratio: float = 0.8) -> Data:
    num_nodes = data.x.size(0)
    num_keep = max(1, int(num_nodes * ratio))

    perm = torch.randperm(num_nodes)[:num_keep]
    perm, _ = perm.sort()

    # Build node mapping
    node_map = torch.full((num_nodes,), -1, dtype=torch.long)
    node_map[perm] = torch.arange(num_keep)

    # Filter edges
    edge_index = data.edge_index
    mask = node_map[edge_index[0]] >= 0
    mask &= node_map[edge_index[1]] >= 0
    new_edge_index = node_map[edge_index[:, mask]]

    new_x = data.x[perm]

import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class SupConLoss(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, temperature: float = 0.07):
        super().__init__()
        self.temperature = temperature

    def forward(self, features: torch.Tensor, labels: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        device = features.device
        bsz, n_views, feat_dim = features.shape

        # Reshape to [bsz * n_views, feat_dim]
        features = features.reshape(bsz * n_views, feat_dim)

        # Compute similarity matrix
        sim = torch.matmul(features, features.T) / self.temperature

        # Mask out self-similarity (diagonal)
        mask_self = torch.eye(bsz * n_views, dtype=torch.bool, device=device)

        # Build positive mask: same label OR same sample (different view)
        labels_expanded = labels.repeat(n_views)  # [bsz * n_views]
        mask_pos = labels_expanded.unsqueeze(0) == labels_expanded.unsqueeze(1)  # [N, N]
        mask_pos = mask_pos & ~mask_self  # exclude self

        # Log-sum-exp trick for numerical stability
        logits_max, _ = sim.detach().max(dim=1, keepdim=True)
        logits = sim - logits_max

        # Compute log-softmax over negatives + positives (excluding self)
        exp_logits = torch.exp(logits)
        exp_logits = exp_logits * (~mask_self).float()
        log_sum_exp = torch.log(exp_logits.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) + 1e-12)

        # Compute mean of log-prob over positives
        log_prob = logits - log_sum_exp
        pos_log_prob = (mask_pos.float() * log_prob).sum(dim=1)
        num_pos = mask_pos.float().sum(dim=1)

        # Avoid division by zero for samples with no positives
        num_pos = torch.clamp(num_pos, min=1.0)
        loss = -(pos_log_prob / num_pos).mean()

        return loss
